Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette:
Rangi Parata is a 63-year-old Māori man, married and working as a senior financial analyst at a mid-sized investment firm in Auckland's financial district. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant deterioration in his functioning over the past eighteen months, tracing back to the night his car was struck by a freight truck on a rural highway outside the city.

It had been a late evening in winter. Rangi had been driving home from a client dinner, the road dark and largely empty. A truck, whose driver had fallen asleep at the wheel, crossed the centre line and hit Rangi's vehicle almost head-on at speed. The impact was catastrophic. His car was spun off the road and came to rest in a drainage ditch, partially submerged. For what felt to Rangi like an eternity - later confirmed to have been over forty minutes - he was trapped in the wreckage in near-total darkness, the engine ticking and groaning around him, the smell of petrol and hot metal filling the cabin. He could hear other vehicles passing on the road above, their engines and tyres audible but their headlights unable to find him in the ditch. He was certain, at several points during those forty minutes, that he was going to die alone in the dark.

He survived with serious but ultimately treatable injuries. Physically, he recovered well. Psychologically, the months that followed told a different story. He returned to work after three months of medical leave, and it was there that the shape of his suffering began to reveal itself. The firm's underground car park, dimly lit at the far end near the stairwell, became something Rangi could not simply walk through. The moment he moved from the brightness of the street into that enclosed, shadowed space, his body would respond before he had formed any conscious thought - heart hammering, breath shortening, legs slowing. He had come to believe that his nervous system simply could not be trusted to wait for his mind to catch up, and this frightened him as much as the dark itself.

The smell of petrol, encountered at a service station or even near a colleague's car, could pull him back into the wreck without warning - not as a recollection he chose to visit, but as something immediate and present, the darkness and the smell and the sounds of the highway above him arriving all at once as though the accident were unfolding again in real time. He would sometimes hear, clearly and involuntarily, the grinding of metal and the distant passing of engines, as vivid as if he were still in the ditch. These moments were not, to Rangi, memories in any ordinary sense. They felt like the present tense.

He had stopped driving at night entirely. He had also, more gradually and more reluctantly, begun avoiding any situation that required him to be in a dark or enclosed space - underground venues, windowless meeting rooms, the cinema he and his wife had visited together regularly for years. His wife, Hinerangi, had at first been patient and accommodating, but the cumulative weight of his withdrawal had begun to strain their relationship. She had asked, carefully and with evident love, whether he was perhaps avoiding things that might actually help him heal. He had not been able to explain to her why thinking about the event felt, to him, like a risk he could not afford to take - that if he allowed himself to go there, he was certain he would not be able to hold himself together.

At work, Rangi had taken to sitting only in seats that faced the door and arriving early enough to identify every exit before colleagues filled the room. He woke most nights in the small hours, lying rigid in the dark beside his sleeping wife, listening and checking. He had come to believe that vigilance was not a burden but a necessity - that the world had revealed itself as a place where catastrophe could arrive without warning, and that the only rational response was to remain perpetually alert.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a morning when he sat in his car in the firm's car park for forty-five minutes, unable to make himself go in. He had sat there, a man of thirty years' professional experience, and wept. What he most hoped for, he said at intake, was to be able to sit in a dark room with his wife and watch a film again. What he most feared was that the person capable of doing that no longer existed.
